chunks: Buck control topologies compared. The question: Explain different control topologies.
A buck controller decides when to switch in one of a few ways. Voltage mode watches only the output voltage. Current mode also watches the inductor current.
Ripple-based schemes, such as hysteretic and constant on-time, just fire a pulse whenever the output drops below a reference.
Each has its own trade-off in simplicity, noise and speed.
Think of three ways to keep a room warm. The first checks only the room thermometer and nudges the heater up or down.
The second also senses how hard the heater is running, so it reacts earlier and can protect itself.
The third is a simple on-off thermostat that switches the heater on whenever the room drops below a set point. They all heat the room, but they respond and behave differently.
Voltage mode. One loop. The error amplifier output is compared with a fixed sawtooth: duty d equals V c over V ramp . The compensator must handle the LC double pole.
Duty cycle: the fraction of each cycle the top switch is on ("What is duty cycle"). Error amplifier: compares the output to the reference.
Compensation: the network that keeps the loop stable ("What stability means in a buck").
Inner current loop: a fast loop around the inductor current in current mode ("Voltage mode vs current mode control").
Constant on-time (COT): a ripple-based scheme that fires a fixed-length pulse when the output is low.
A 3. 3 volts output sags a little. In voltage mode, the error amplifier output rises and a wider pulse comes at the next tick of the controller's clock.
In peak current mode, the error amplifier raises the current threshold, so the next pulse runs longer before the switch turns off.
In a constant-on-time controller, a fixed-length pulse fires as soon as the output crosses below the reference, with no waiting for a clock. That is the whole idea.
"I group buck control by when the controller decides to switch.
Voltage mode compares an error amplifier output to a fixed ramp: simple and quiet, but a second-order plant needs type III compensation.
Current mode adds an inner inductor-current loop, which makes the plant first-order, rejects line changes and gives cycle-by-cycle current limit, but needs slope compensation and is noise-sensitive.
Ripple-based schemes like hysteretic and constant on-time have no compensation and respond very fast, but the frequency varies. Digital control adds flexibility.
I'd choose by transient needs, noise, capacitor type and simplicity."
